Today’s story is all about my recent terrace garden harvest! 🌿🌞
As we come to the end of summer, some of these veggies mark the final harvest of the season—while a few like amaranthus just don’t seem to leave my garden! They pop up here and there, and I let a few grow fully while leaving others for seeds. You’ll spot them in today’s harvest.

Sorrel varieties are also in the basket—you just need to keep plucking and pinching them. They reward you by branching out and being ready for the next harvest in just a week!
A special mention goes to ponaganti kura—a complete invader in my garden. It claims every container by simply touching the soil and rooting at every node. While it’s nutritious, removing it is such a task—it’s rooted deep and keeps popping back up no matter what!

I’ve also harvested a few volunteer ash gourds. These sprouted from seeds I added while layering compost two months ago. They grew over the compost and flourished just in time before the rainy season kicked in—my bonus crops!

And oh, the dragon fruits—they only need water and no other care. Yet, they reward me year after year! 🍉🌵

This time, I’ve also added a new variety—elephant tusk okra (Tusk okra)—and have transplanted them along with cucumbers. The cucumbers are now cleared, and these okras have taken over those containers.

So, today’s harvest is a perfect example of how you can continue growing food without any break between seasons. If you’d like to understand the process in detail, I’ve pinned the video in the comments & story.🌱

Do check it out—especially if you’re interested in growing your own food.

These French climbing beans are one of the last things left in the greenhouse that require planting outdoors. For the first year ever, I will have finished planting out before the 1st June. But with the mild weather and an early last frost date (in my area) I took the calculated risk to get as many plants as possible out of pots and into the ground. Every growing year is different and this year I’ve scheduled the gardening around the weather, parenting and work. I’m grateful to the weather for holding out and allowing me to get everything planted ahead of schedule 🌞🌾

So far, everything looks to be well and there are early signs of young fruit already on the way. Here’s hoping for a plentiful season! 🌿🌼

I cut a handful of blooms to enjoy indoors, even though it’s a total dilemma. My growing season is short and seed heads take 4 to 6 weeks to mature, which means this is the time I should be letting everything go to seed, not cutting or deadheading.

Still… how could I resist these? Some of my absolute favorites from this season. I really hope they give me some stellar seedlings next year.

I downsized a lot this year, from over 250 cultivars to around 100 (maybe?). I really need to get better at logging inventory 🥴. Next season I might grow even fewer, focusing just on the ones that match my breeding goals.

Growing seedlings is such a fun and chaotic adventure. I had to cut all the singles this year. The hardest ones to say goodbye to were probably Rhubarb and Custard and Orange Hype. I’m also only growing a few waterlily types right now.

I’m still super new to all this “hybridizing” stuff and learning as I go. I don’t breed for show, so ADS standards aren’t really my thing. I’m a solution architect by day and a pretend flower farmer by night, there is no method to my madness.  Anyone else chaos planting? 😆🤣

I spent the day volunteering at Rhythm Seed Farm, @rhythmseedfarm an urban nonprofit seed farm here in the city. One of the first things I did was plant into the soil. Rhythm Seed Farm isn’t just growing vegetables, flowers, and medicine, they’re growing human connection and community.

Urban gardens like this are frontline spaces for building the future we want to see. In a system shaped by industrial agriculture and food deserts, planting a seed becomes a revolutionary act. It’s about reclaiming our right to grow, to feed our neighbors, and to heal the land from the ground up.

Organic Gardening Advantages and Disadvantages

Advantages:

Adapts to long and varied growing seasons

Improves local clay soil

Enhances biodiversity

Reduces the need for synthetic fertilizers and pesticides, saving money over time.

Disadvantages:

Increased labor for pest and weed control.

Specific pests may require intensive management.

Soil amendments are labor-intensive.

Drought conditions mean organic gardeners must be water-wise.

High summer heat may stress plants, requiring careful plant selection and watering schedules

Want to maximize your fall harvest? 🥕✨

Pairing the right crops together is the secret to healthier plants and fewer pests—no chemicals needed!

These powerhouse combos thrive in cool-season beds:

🥬 Cabbage + Dill → Dill attracts beneficial insects that protect cabbage.

🌱 Peas + Turnips → Peas enrich the soil while turnips mature fast below.

🥦 Broccoli + Celery → Both love cool weather and share moisture needs.

🥗 Lettuce + Beets → Lettuce shades the soil while beets grow deep.

🧄 Garlic + Kale → Garlic deters pests, and kale keeps producing into winter.

🌿 Spinach + Radishes → Radishes mature early, leaving room for spinach.

🥕 Carrots + Onions → Perfect partners—different root depths and natural pest defense.

🍂 Quick Tip: Companion planting saves space, reduces pests, and boosts harvest flavor.

Some garden truths aren’t found in seed packets or how-to videos.

They’re learned by doing—by paying attention. Here are the lessons that stick with you long after harvest.

💧 Moving water is magic.
It invites life—frogs, birds, dragonflies—and oxygenates your space. A small fountain or stream makes your garden pulse with energy.

🌿 Vertical growing is essential.
Limited on space? Go up. Vining crops love it, airflow improves, and harvests become easier. Every layer of space can grow something.

🔁 Succession plant everything.
When one plant’s done, another goes in. This rhythm keeps beds productive and pollinators busy. Food and flowers alike—don’t let soil sit bare.

🌈 Variety brings resilience.
Monocultures are fragile. Mix colors, bloom times, species. Heirlooms + hybrids, annuals + perennials—intentional variety builds a bulletproof ecosystem.

🌱 Soil is everything.
Forget quick fixes. Compost, mulch, microbes—this is where life begins. Feed the soil, and the soil will feed the garden.

👣 The gardener’s shadow is the best fertilizer.
Presence matters. Walk, observe, touch, listen. The more you see, the better you respond. Your care is what cultivates abundance.

🌸 No flowers = no food.
Veggies depend on pollinators. Pollinators depend on blooms. Interplant flowers not just for beauty, but for the bees. It’s all connected.

🦋 Diversity = biodiversity.
Each plant invites different life. Together, they form a balanced, resilient web. More species = fewer problems and more joy.

🪺 A garden is an ecosystem.
It’s not just plants—it’s bugs, birds, bacteria, weather. Build relationships between living things, and watch your garden stabilize.

🎨 Plants don’t care about pretty.
They care about what helps them grow: soil, light, water. Ditch perfection. Embrace wild, messy, working beauty.

🐛 If nothing’s eating your garden… that’s a problem.
A garden with no pests is a garden with no predators. A few holes mean your ecosystem is alive and working as it should.

From my garden to yours,

🌸Erin

Chard! 🌱 

This sunset chard has been lighting up the allotment since last year and is growing so much with the warm weather we’ve been having! 

Chard, which is also known as Swiss chard, is a leafy green vegetable with a mild, slightly sweet taste, similar to spinach but with a stronger flavor. It’s a member of the beet family and has large, crinkled leaves attached to thick, crunchy stems. 

You can eat chard raw in salads, cooked like spinach, or used in various dishes. I like to use mine in pasta dishes, stews and casseroles and in wraps as a green leaf. 

I start my chard seeds off in the greenhouse in early spring and I multi sow them which means I sow more than one seed in each module. When they are around 5cm tall I garden them off and plant them out. I’ll then do another sowing, directly into the growing site, around July/August to overwinter giving me crops through winter and into early spring and the hungry gap.

Those little green nuggets? Yep… hornworm poop. 🐛 And if you see it, you’ve got a tomato thief hiding out, blending in like a pro.

Step 2️⃣ Clear away the poops.

Let’s get specific, What to plant in July & August (local subtropical region)

I get asked this all the time 
 “What can I grow here?”
“Why are my plants dying?”

The truth is, what works in one part of the country might fail miserably somewhere else.
We’re subtropical here, and as always timing matters, especially in winter!

Right now (July & August) we’re at the tail end of our cool season seed planting, (mine were planted Feb/ March ) but there’s still plenty you can sow from seed to make the most of it….

🥬 Veggies
– Lettuce
– Kale
– Silverbeet
– Carrots

– Snow peas

– Radish

🌸 Flowers
– Calendula
– Violas
– Nasturtiums

Planting in the right season sets you up for success, healthy plants, fewer pests, and actual harvests. 🌿
Just because it’s for sale in a seed packet doesn’t mean it will grow well right now where you are, if at all! Take Rhubarb… it might grow for a while but I’ve never had much success in subtropical conditions! It likes the cold! 

Stick with what suits our local climate now and you’ll be harvesting before spring even begins….

Which African bird would drive you nuts…hadedas (ibis) in video one or guinea fowl in the second? 😅

Uhhmmm that is 7 heads of cauliflower!!! 🙈 Not quite @poodles_and_produce success but grateful nonetheless with eggplants, chillies and cherry tomatoes in winter to go with all the citrus. 

My caulis are still a win because life and sickness got in the way and they lived in seed punnets for way too long. I didn’t expect much, but direct sowed more seed 2 weeks ago in a 15cm empty row gap in my raised bed. That’s all the space you need and can transplant out from there. (Bonus succession crop)

You don’t always need soil and seed trays. Sowing can be made simple as long as the temperature is correct for what you are sowing. I always check germination temperatures for everything I sow. No use sowing seeds which need cold stratification on a heat mat for instance. I even move those seed trays outside to get the cold somewhere where they won’t get too washed out and waterlogged from rain. 

Once again my pots on soil method works. Seed trays placed in your beds (some under big leaf plant protection) allows the microbes to assist germination and the soil below regulates the moisture. 

Have any of you tried my pots on living soil trick yet? I can’t tell you how well it works and I even have unplanted trees and a full grapevine still in pots which they bust right out of. As much as I hate plastic, they work better than terracotta or cement pots.

Peppers are still popping here on the Ridge! I love these Trident Poblano peppers, they’re crazy performers. I’ve grown them the last 3 seasons and they do better each year.

Here’s something a lot of folks don’t realize: peppers are actually perennials. Yep, if you overwinter them, they’ll come back stronger the next season. Saves time, boosts production, and lets you get a head start.

Simple rules for overwintering peppers:
• Before frost, dig them up carefully and pot them in fresh soil.
• Cut them back to just a few strong stems.
• Keep them in a sunny window or under a grow light.
• Water lightly, just enough to keep the roots alive.

Come spring, they’ll bounce right back and reward you with earlier, heavier harvests.

For tiden starter jeg hver dag (efter morgenkaffen selvfølgelig) med at gå en runde i haven og opsamle nedfaldsæbler - hvis jeg ikke når det, risikerer robotplæneklipperen nemlig at få forstoppelse. Nogle æbler ryger ind til hønsene og andre ryger i komposten, mens de rimelig fejlfrie ryger ind i huset. Her på det sidste er der kommet et nyt sted at gøre af dem - de ryger i mistbænken under peberplanterne. Peberplanterne står bare frit uden overdækning, og med de faldende temperaturer nu hvor vi kommer ind i efteråret, går modningen af de runde, æblelignende peberfrugter stedse langsommere. Rådnende æbler har den gavnlige funktion at de udskiller etylen, som netop fremmer modningen af frugt. Dermed kan vores overflod af rådne æbler gøre nytte: vi får flere modne peber inden efterårskulden sætter en stopper for udviklingen.

🌿 New to veggie gardening? Start strong with these must-know tips! 🥕✨

1️⃣Location is everything! Your veggies need 6–8 hours of sun, so pick a spot that shines.

2️⃣Know your zone. Not all plants thrive everywhere—check your USDA zone before planting.

3️⃣Feed your soil, not just your plants. Healthy soil = healthy harvest. Add compost and rotate crops each season.

4️⃣Welcome the bugs! 🌸 Marigolds, nasturtiums, and zinnias attract pollinators & beneficial insects. Skip the chemicals and let nature help.

5️⃣Harvest early and often. It encourages more growth and keeps your garden producing longer.

6️⃣And finally—don’t stress! Gardening is part science, part art, and 100% learning. Every “oops” is just future wisdom in disguise 🌱💚

You know what brings me joy after a long day? A handful of homegrown food that grew itself. As a professional gardener, I need my personal gardens to tend themselves as much as possible in a more permaculture style of garden. Alas, I usually only have a few hours a week I can devote to them. The trick is to let things seed themselves, let things grow over the winter, to not be too aggressive about turning your beds over in the spring, and know your baby veggie plants so you avoid weeding them. Plants often plant themselves where they want to grow! I do delineate areas for summer crops, but let the perennial and self seeders fill the edges.

Here are some of my spring favorites for the autopilot garden: French sorrel, arugula, parsley, cilantro, overwintered kale/collards, chives, chard, and mustard greens. I haven't really planted any of these in years. I do spread cilantro and arugula seeds around from time to time. It can take a season or two for things to establish, and you have to be ok with letting a few bolt and seed everywhere.

🌷 How to plant a bulb lasagne 🌷
A bulb lasagne (or layered planting) is a brilliant way to get months of colour from one pot – and our Bulb Compost is perfect for the job. Here’s how:
1️⃣ Choose a deep pot with drainage holes.
2️⃣ Add a layer of Bulb Compost to the bottom.
3️⃣ Place your largest, latest-flowering bulbs (tulips work well). Cover with more compost.
4️⃣ Add a middle layer with bulbs like daffodils or hyacinths. Cover again.
5️⃣ Top with the earliest bulbs (crocus or dwarf iris). Finish with another layer of compost.
6️⃣ Water well and leave the pot in a sheltered spot until spring.
🌼 The result? A staggered display of blooms from early spring right through to early summer – all in one container.
Our peat-free Bulb Compost gives bulbs the drainage, nutrients and structure they need to thrive year after year.

Let’s talk water 💧… because it’s not just how much, but how and when that matters.

In our Queensland climate, watering smart makes all the difference, not just for plant health, but for saving time and avoiding disease.

Here are a few simple tips that work in our subtropical gardens! 

☀️ Water early in the morning, before the heat kicks in. It gives plants time to soak it up before the sun gets too strong, and helps prevent fungal problems that come from damp overnight leaves.

🌿 Water the soil, not the leaves, aim low and slow. Drippers, soaker hoses, or a watering can right at the base are perfect. Wet leaves and humidity is the perfect storm for disease.

🪴 Mulch makes all the difference,  it keeps moisture in the soil longer, reduces how often you need to water, and helps regulate soil temps too.

💧 Deep and less often is better than a daily sprinkle, encourage strong roots by giving the soil a good soak, rather than just wetting the surface. And check.. make sure that soil is nice and wet under the mulch! 

Every garden is a little different, but understanding how water works with your soil, mulch, plants and climate can make all the difference.

We’re on rainwater here, and we top up the garden tank from the dam when needed, so every drop counts. 🌧️💧

How long is it before the previously respected gardening practices and advice go out of fashion or are surpassed by more modern methods meaning your old faithful gardening books are out of date?

I have a 1991 copy of Geoff Hamilton's "Successful Organic Gardening" and in it he talks about the importance of digging the soil to free up compacted ground and allow air and water to pass through the soil.

But now there seems to be a movement towards the "no dig" method with even the R.H.S. promoting it and using it at Wisley. It says "Now, scientific evidence shows us that [digging] damages soil structure and disrupts the natural processes that occur within it. This makes no-dig a better choice for soil health by minimising disturbance." [see this page: https://www.rhs.org.uk/soil-composts-mulches/no-dig-gardening]

I realise a lot of the information from 1991 probably is still valid but glad I double checked about no dig before spending hours in the garden with my spade.

Think of mulch as the guardian of the soil food web. It reduces moisture loss and keeps soil cool by shielding it from the sun, fostering the conditions soil organisms need to thrive. If soil health is lacking, or some key elements are absent, it can't properly sustain plant life.

In Central Texas, it’s more important now than ever to provide mulch for mature native trees, as persistent droughts continue to threaten their livelihood. When mulching trees, be generous and add 2–3 inches all around the canopy. The wider an area you can cover, the better!

Mulch will break down over time, so don’t worry about overdoing it. Just be sure to leave a couple of inches around the base of the tree with no mulch so the root flair can breathe, and to reduce the risk of disease.

By feeding your soil with natural inputs and protecting it with mulch, you’ll support and champion a living system that, in turn, will sustain you and ensure that future generations have shade.

Organic Gardening is a huge subject, far too much to include here. As September is Organic Gardening month, we've put together a short overview. 🌿

Origins • Pioneered in the 1940s by British agronomist Sir Albert Howard • Developed for farmers who couldn't afford expensive synthetic amendments • Based on natural soil cycles rather than petroleum-based products

Core Principles • Use only naturally-derived materials, no synthetic substances • Focus on building soil health as the foundation • Strengthen plants' natural defenses against pests and diseases

Soil Health Practices • Compost organic waste and kitchen scraps • Add organic matter regularly to improve soil structure • Avoid synthetic fertilizers and chemical amendments

Pest and Weed Control • Use botanical insecticides and soaps instead of chemicals • Apply cultural controls like mulching and cultivation • Rely on strong, healthy plants to naturally resist problems 

Benefits • Creates sustainable growing cycle • Reduces dependency on external inputs • Builds long-term soil fertility and plant health 🐝
